newsitem.title: GERMANY: EU's de Silguy sees most EU states launching euro.
newsitem.headline: EU's de Silguy sees most EU states launching euro.

text.p: European economic affairs commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy said on Tuesday that most European Union countries should be in a position to take part in the launch of the single currency in January 1999.
De Silguy, addressing the Global 24 European Monetary Union conference, also said would-be participants in the euro would have to show permanent and realistic consolidation of public finances.

"Progress with economic convergence and the market upturn in GDP growth (which should amount to 2.4 percent this year compared with 1.6 percent last year) encourage me to believe ... that a majority of member states will be capable of participating in the euro from the start," De Silguy said in the text of a speech which was released in advance.

De Silguy, sharing a panel with top international central bankers, also said that European Union member states must continue their efforts to rein in their finances to meet the convergence criteria set down in the Maastricht Treaty.

The treaty calls on states to cut their budget deficits to three percent of gross domestic product (GDP), or show significant progress toward that figure, and their national debts to sixty percent of GDP.

"Participating countries will have to achieve a high degree of sustainable convergence. One-off measures designed to cut deficits in 1997 alone will have to be complemented or replaced by other, permanent, measures," De Silguy said.
"In a word, consolidation of public finances must be a permanent reality and not an accounting device. The credibility of the euro depends on full application of all the conditions in the Treaty."

De Silguy also said the stability and growth pact designed to enforce fiscal discipline in the euro zone, which was ratified last month in Amsterdam, would ensure permanently low interest rates that would be conducive to investment, growth and employment.
"It is clear that sound macroeconomic and fiscal policies go hand in hand with strong, job-creating growth," he said.

The assessment of which countries can take part in the euro, which will be made following recommendations from the European Commission and from the European Monetary Institute, would be based on the economic criteria alone, De Silguy said.
He said the size of a country or scale of its population would not play any role.

The three main priorities in the run-up to the euro launch would be reinforcing economic policy co-ordination, clarifying arrangements for the external management of the euro and solving the practical problems associated with the single currency.
These practical issues included fixing conversion rates between the euro and participating currencies and fixing a schedule for the introduction of euro notes and coins.
"Precise answers to all of these questions need to be clear by next March to enable decisions to be taken in late April or early May 1998 when the first participating countries are chosen."
